---
title: "Quiz: the Haar transform"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. By hand, a Haar step replaces a pair $(a, b)$ by $s = (a+b)/2$ and $d = (a-b)/2$; the orthonormal version uses $1/\sqrt2$ instead of $1/2$.

---

**Q1.** A signal is zero except for one spike. Its Fourier magnitudes are all equal. Where in the Fourier coefficients is the position of the spike?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Magnitudes and phases.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In the **phases**: a spike at $n_0$ has $X_k = e^{-2\pi i k n_0/N}$, magnitude 1 for every $k$, phase $-2\pi k n_0/N$. The position is spread over all coefficients together; no single coefficient says "here".
:::

---

**Q2.** Why can a short-time Fourier transform with one window size not resolve both a sharp edge and a slow wave well?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a short window contain of a slow wave? What does a long window do to the edge?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A short window locates the edge, but contains only a fraction of a cycle of the slow wave, so its frequency cannot be determined. A long window contains many cycles, but smears the edge over the window length. Position and frequency resolution trade off against each other (uncertainty relation); wavelets use short windows for high frequencies and long windows for low ones.
:::

---

**Q3.** Compute the Haar transform (by hand, $1/2$) of $(3, 5, 5, 3)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two levels: averages and differences of the pairs, then of the two averages.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Level 1: averages $(4, 4)$, differences $(-1, 1)$. Level 2: average $4$, difference $0$. Result $(4 \mid 0 \mid -1, 1)$. Check: $4 \pm 0 = (4, 4)$; $4 \pm (-1) = (3, 5)$, $4 \pm 1 = (5, 3)$.
:::

---

**Q4.** Invert the by-hand Haar transform $(10 \mid 2 \mid 1, -1)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$a = s + d$, $b = s - d$, coarse to fine.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$10 \pm 2 = (12, 8)$; then $12 \pm 1 = (13, 11)$ and $8 \pm (-1) = (7, 9)$: $x = (13, 11, 7, 9)$.
:::

---

**Q5.** Which of these signals of 8 samples has the fewest nonzero Haar coefficients: a constant, a spike, a ramp, a step between samples 4 and 5?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A Haar pattern gives zero when it sees a constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The constant: 1 (only the average). The step exactly in the middle: 2 (the average and the coarsest detail). The spike: 4 ($\log_2 8 + 1$). The ramp: all 8, because every pattern sees a slope.
:::

---

**Q6.** With the orthonormal Haar transform, a signal has coefficients $(10, -4, 3, 0, 1, 0, -1, 0)$. You keep the two largest. What is the squared error, without reconstructing?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
In an orthonormal basis the error is the sum of the dropped squares.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Keep $10$ and $-4$; drop $3, 1, -1$ (and the zeros): $9 + 1 + 1 = 11$.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why does the by-hand normalisation $s = (a+b)/2$ not preserve $\sum x^2$, while $(a+b)/\sqrt2$ does?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare $s^2 + d^2$ with $a^2 + b^2$ for one pair.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With $1/2$: $s^2 + d^2 = \tfrac14\big((a+b)^2 + (a-b)^2\big) = \tfrac12(a^2 + b^2)$, half the energy per step. With $1/\sqrt2$: $\tfrac12\big((a+b)^2 + (a-b)^2\big) = a^2 + b^2$. The normalised step is an orthogonal $2\times2$ matrix, a rotation plus a reflection.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the Haar basis vectors $(1, 1, -1, -1)/2$ and $(1, -1, 0, 0)/\sqrt2$ are orthogonal, and explain in words why any two Haar patterns at different levels are orthogonal.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where the short pattern is nonzero, what does the long one look like?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Dot product: $\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}(1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot (-1) + 0 + 0) = 0$. In general, a finer pattern lies entirely inside one half of a coarser pattern, where the coarser one is constant. The dot product is then that constant times the sum of the finer pattern, which is zero ($+$ and $-$ halves cancel). Two patterns at the same level do not overlap.
:::
